title: Unlearnable phases of matter
summary: We identify fundamental limitations in machine learning by demonstrating that non-trivial mixed-state phases of matter are computationally hard to learn. Focusing on unsupervised learning of distributions, we show that autoregressive neural networks fail to learn global properties of distributions characterized by locally indistinguishable (LI) states. We demonstrate that conditional mutual information (CMI) is a useful diagnostic for LI: we show that for classical distributions, long-range CMI of a state implies a spatially LI partner. By introducing a restricted statistical query model, we prove that nontrivial phases with long-range CMI, such as strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking phases, are hard to learn. We validate our claims by using recurrent, convolutional, and Transformer neural networks to learn the syndrome and physical distributions of toric/surface code under bit flip noise. Our findings suggest hardness of learning as a diagnostic tool for detecting mixed-state phases and transitions and error-correction thresholds, and they suggest CMI and more generally ``non-local Gibbsness'' as metrics for how hard a distribution is to learn.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates fundamental limitations in machine learning by showing that non-trivial mixed-state phases of matter are computationally hard to learn, with autoregressive neural networks failing to learn global properties of distributions characterized by locally indistinguishable states.
AI.motivation: To identify fundamental limitations in machine learning by examining whether non-trivial mixed-state phases of matter can be learned, and to understand the relationship between computational hardness of learning and physical properties of distributions.
AI.method: 1) Show autoregressive neural networks fail to learn global properties of locally indistinguishable (LI) state distributions; 2) Demonstrate conditional mutual information (CMI) as diagnostic for LI states; 3) Introduce restricted statistical query model to prove hardness of learning nontrivial phases with long-range CMI; 4) Validate with recurrent, convolutional, and Transformer neural networks on toric/surface code distributions under bit flip noise.
AI.result: 1) Non-trivial mixed-state phases with long-range CMI (like strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking phases) are computationally hard to learn; 2) CMI serves as useful diagnostic for locally indistinguishable states; 3) Neural networks fail to learn global properties of LI state distributions; 4) Hardness of learning can serve as diagnostic tool for detecting mixed-state phases, transitions, and error-correction thresholds.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes fundamental limitations in machine learning for certain physical systems, proposes hardness of learning as diagnostic for mixed-state phases and transitions, and suggests CMI and "non-local Gibbsness" as metrics for quantifying how hard a distribution is to learn.

title: Krylov space perturbation theory for quantum synchronization in closed systems
summary: Strongly interacting quantum many-body systems are expected to thermalize, however, some evade thermalization due to symmetries. Quantum synchronization provides one such example of ergodicity breaking, but previous studies have focused on open systems. Here, motivated by the problem of ergodicity breaking in closed systems and the study of non-trivial dynamics, we investigate synchronization in a closed disordered Heisenberg spin chain. In the presence of large random disorder, strongly breaking the permutation symmetry of the system, we observe the emergence of spatial synchronization, where spins lock into locally synchronized patches. This behavior can be interpreted as a fragmentation of the global dynamical symmetry $S^+$ into a collection of local dynamical symmetries, each characterized by a distinct frequency. In the weak-disorder regime, still without permutation symmetry, we show that the synchronization mechanism can be understood perturbatively within Krylov space. In the absence of disorder, the Krylov space associated with the dynamical symmetry $S^+$ is two-dimensional. Introducing disorder couples this subspace to the remainder of the Krylov space. This coupling leads only to a second-order correction to the frequency of the dynamical symmetry, thereby preserving coherent oscillations despite the presence of small disorder. At stronger disorder, the perturbation modifies $S^+$ so that it acquires a finite lifetime, providing an example of a transient dynamical symmetry.

AI.tldr: Closed disordered Heisenberg spin chains exhibit quantum synchronization as ergodicity breaking, with spatial synchronization emerging at strong disorder and perturbative preservation of coherent oscillations at weak disorder.
AI.motivation: To investigate ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems through quantum synchronization, moving beyond previous open-system studies, and to understand non-trivial dynamics in disordered spin chains.
AI.method: Study synchronization in a closed disordered Heisenberg spin chain, analyzing strong and weak disorder regimes. Use Krylov space perturbation theory for weak disorder, and examine fragmentation of global dynamical symmetry S⁺ into local dynamical symmetries for strong disorder.
AI.result: Strong disorder leads to spatial synchronization with spins locking into locally synchronized patches, interpreted as fragmentation of global dynamical symmetry S⁺ into local dynamical symmetries with distinct frequencies. Weak disorder preserves coherent oscillations through only second-order frequency corrections in Krylov space perturbation theory. Strong disorder creates transient dynamical symmetries with finite lifetimes.
AI.conclusion: Quantum synchronization provides a mechanism for ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems, with disorder strength determining whether synchronization is preserved perturbatively or emerges as spatial fragmentation of dynamical symmetries.

title: Notes on Bell states and quantum teleportation
summary: Bell states and quantum teleportation play important roles in the study of quantum information and computation. But a comprehensive theoretical research on both of them remains to be performed. This work aims to investigate important algebraic properties of generalized Bell states as well as explore topological features of quantum teleportation. First, the basis theorem and basis group are introduced to explain that the extension of a generalized Bell basis by a unitary matrix is still an orthonormal basis. Then a twist operator is defined to make a connection between a generalized multiple qubit Bell state and a tensor product of two qubit Bell state. Besides them, the Temperley--Lieb algebra, the braid group relation and the Yang--Baxter equation are used to provide a topological diagrammatic description of generalized Bell states and quantum teleportation. It turns out that our approach is able to present a clear illustration of relevant quantum information protocols and exhibit a topological nature of quantum entanglement and quantum teleportation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates algebraic properties of generalized Bell states and topological features of quantum teleportation using basis theorems, twist operators, Temperley-Lieb algebra, braid groups, and Yang-Baxter equations to provide topological diagrammatic descriptions.
AI.motivation: Despite the importance of Bell states and quantum teleportation in quantum information and computation, there remains a need for comprehensive theoretical research on both topics, particularly regarding their algebraic properties and topological features.
AI.method: The authors introduce basis theorems and basis groups to show that unitary extensions of generalized Bell bases remain orthonormal. They define twist operators to connect generalized multi-qubit Bell states with tensor products of two-qubit Bell states. They employ Temperley-Lieb algebra, braid group relations, and Yang-Baxter equations to develop topological diagrammatic descriptions of generalized Bell states and quantum teleportation.
AI.result: The approach successfully provides clear illustrations of relevant quantum information protocols and reveals the topological nature of quantum entanglement and quantum teleportation through diagrammatic representations.
AI.conclusion: The topological framework using algebraic structures offers a powerful tool for understanding and visualizing quantum information processes, demonstrating that quantum entanglement and teleportation have inherent topological characteristics that can be systematically described using mathematical tools from knot theory and algebra.

title: Stratified Sampling for Quasi-Probability Decompositions
summary:
Quasi-probability decompositions (QPDs) have proven essential in many quantum algorithms and protocols -- one replaces a ``difficult'' quantum circuit with an ensemble of ``easier'' circuit variants whose weighted outcomes reproduce any target observable. This, however, inevitably yields an increased configuration variance beyond Born-rule shot noise. We develop a broad framework for accounting for and reducing this variance and prove that stratified sampling -- under ideal proportional allocation -- results in an unbiased estimator with a variance that is never worse than naïve sampling (with equality only in degenerate cases).
  Furthermore, we provide a classical dynamic programme to enable stratification on arbitrary product-form QPDs. Numerical simulations of typical QPDs, such as Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) and Probabilistic Angle Interpolation (PAI), demonstrate constant-factor reductions in overall variance (up to $\sim 60$--$80\%$ in an oracle model) and robust $\sim 10\%$ savings in the pessimistic single-shot regime. Our results can be applied immediately to reduce the net sampling cost of practically relevant QPDs that are commonly used in near term and early fault-tolerant algorithms without requiring additional quantum resources.

AI.tldr: Stratified sampling reduces variance in quasi-probability decompositions (QPDs) like PEC and PAI without extra quantum resources, achieving up to 60-80% variance reduction in ideal cases and ~10% in single-shot regimes.
AI.motivation: QPDs are essential for quantum algorithms but increase configuration variance beyond Born-rule shot noise, requiring methods to reduce this variance without additional quantum resources.
AI.method: Developed a framework for variance accounting and reduction using stratified sampling with ideal proportional allocation, plus a classical dynamic program for stratification on arbitrary product-form QPDs.
AI.result: Stratified sampling yields unbiased estimators with variance never worse than naïve sampling. Simulations show constant-factor variance reductions (up to 60-80% in oracle model) and robust ~10% savings in single-shot regimes.
AI.conclusion: The method can immediately reduce sampling costs for practical QPDs used in near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms without requiring additional quantum resources.

title: Quantum computing with anyons is fault tolerant
summary: In seminal work (arxiv:quant-ph/9707021) Alexei Kitaev proposed topological quantum computing (arXiv:cond-mat/0010440, arxiv:quant-ph/9707021, arXiv:quant-ph/0001108, arXiv:0707.1889), whereby logic gates of a quantum computer are conducted by creating, braiding and fusing anyonic particles on a two-dimensional plane. Furthermore, he showed the proposal is inherently robust to local perturbations (arXiv:cond-mat/0010440, arxiv:quant-ph/9707021, arXiv:1001.0344, arXiv:1001.4363) when anyons are created as quasiparticle excitations of a topologically ordered lattice model prepared at zero temperature. Over the decades following this proposal there have been considerable technological developments towards the construction of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Rather than maintaining some target ground state at zero temperature, a modern approach is to actively correct the errors a target state experiences, where we use noisy quantum circuit elements to identify and subsequently correct for deviations from the ideal state. We present an error-correction scheme that enables us to carry out robust universal quantum computation by braiding anyons. We show that our scheme can be carried out on a suitably large device with an arbitrarily small failure rate assuming circuit elements are below some threshold level of local noise. The error-corrected scheme we have developed therefore enables us to carry out fault-tolerant topological quantum computation using modern quantum hardware that is now under development.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an error-correction scheme enabling fault-tolerant topological quantum computation using anyon braiding on modern quantum hardware, achieving arbitrarily small failure rates with noise below threshold.
AI.motivation: Kitaev's topological quantum computing proposal using anyon braiding is inherently robust to local perturbations but requires zero-temperature ground states. Modern quantum hardware uses active error correction rather than maintaining ground states, creating a need to bridge topological computing with contemporary error-correction approaches.
AI.method: Developed an error-correction scheme that enables robust universal quantum computation through anyon braiding. The method uses noisy quantum circuit elements to identify and correct deviations from ideal states, operating on suitably large devices.
AI.result: The scheme achieves arbitrarily small failure rates assuming circuit elements are below a threshold level of local noise. This enables fault-tolerant topological quantum computation using modern quantum hardware currently under development.
AI.conclusion: The error-corrected scheme successfully bridges Kitaev's topological quantum computing paradigm with modern active error-correction approaches, enabling fault-tolerant topological quantum computation on contemporary quantum hardware platforms.

title: Efficient Simulation of Pre-Born-Oppenheimer Dynamics on a Quantum Computer
summary: In this work, we present a quantum algorithm for direct first-principles simulation of electron-nuclear dynamics on a first-quantized real-space grid. Our algorithm achieves best-in-class efficiency for block-encoding the pre-Born-Oppenheimer molecular Hamiltonian by harnessing the linear scaling of swap networks for implementing the quadratic number of particle interactions, while using a novel alternating sign implementation of the Coulomb interaction that exploits highly optimized arithmetic routines. We benchmark our approach for a series of scientifically and industrially relevant chemical reactions. We demonstrate over an order-of-magnitude reduction in costs compared to previous state-of-the-art for the $\rm NH_3+BF_3$ reaction, achieving a Toffoli cost of $8.7\times10^{9}$ per femtosecond using $1362$ logical qubits (system + ancillas). Our results significantly lower the resources required for fault-tolerant simulations of photochemical reactions, while providing a suite of algorithmic primitives that are expected to serve as foundational building blocks for a broader class of quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for first-principles electron-nuclear dynamics with best-in-class efficiency using swap networks and novel Coulomb interaction implementation, achieving 10× cost reduction for chemical reactions.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient fault-tolerant quantum simulations of photochemical reactions by developing a quantum algorithm that significantly reduces computational costs for first-principles electron-nuclear dynamics simulations.
AI.method: Uses a quantum algorithm for direct first-principles simulation on a first-quantized real-space grid, employing swap networks for linear scaling of particle interactions and a novel alternating sign implementation of Coulomb interaction with optimized arithmetic routines.
AI.result: Demonstrated over an order-of-magnitude reduction in costs compared to previous state-of-the-art for the NH₃+BF₃ reaction, achieving Toffoli cost of 8.7×10⁹ per femtosecond using 1362 logical qubits (system + ancillas).
AI.conclusion: The algorithm significantly lowers resources required for fault-tolerant simulations of photochemical reactions and provides foundational building blocks for broader quantum algorithms.

title: Superresolution in Quantum Noise Spectroscopy via Filter Design
summary: Resolving signals with closely spaced frequencies is central to applications in communications, spectroscopy and sensing. Recent results have shown that quantum sensing protocols can exhibit superresolution, the ability to discriminate between spectral lines with arbitrarily small frequency separation. Here, we revisit this problem from the perspective of quantum control theory, utilizing the filter function formalism to derive general, analytic conditions on quantum control protocols for achieving superresolution. Building on these conditions, we develop an optimal control framework, the utility of which is demonstrated through numerical identification of superresolution control protocols in the presence of realistic, experimentally-relevant constraints. We further extend our results to entangled initial states and assess their potential advantage. Our approach is broadly applicable to a wide variety of quantum sensing platforms, and it provides a systematic path to discover novel protocols that surpass conventional resolution limits in these systems.

AI.tldr: Quantum control framework enables superresolution sensing beyond conventional limits through analytic conditions and optimal control design.
AI.motivation: Resolving closely spaced frequencies is crucial for communications, spectroscopy, and sensing applications, but conventional methods face resolution limits. Quantum sensing offers potential for superresolution but lacks systematic design approaches.
AI.method: Utilizes quantum control theory and filter function formalism to derive analytic conditions for superresolution. Develops optimal control framework with numerical identification of protocols under realistic constraints. Extends to entangled initial states.
AI.result: Established general analytic conditions for achieving superresolution in quantum sensing. Demonstrated practical control protocols through numerical optimization that work under experimental constraints. Assessed potential advantages of entangled states.
AI.conclusion: Provides systematic framework for designing quantum control protocols that surpass conventional resolution limits, broadly applicable to various quantum sensing platforms and enabling discovery of novel superresolution techniques.

title: Bosonic statistics enhance Maxwell's demon in photonic experiment
comment: 4.5 pages (3 figures) + appendices (10.5 pages / 3 figures / 2 tables)
summary: Maxwell's demon elucidates the value of information in thermodynamics, using measurement and feedback: he evolves an equilibrated gas into a nonequilibrium state, from which one might extract work. The demon can evolve the system farther from equilibrium, on average, if the particles obey Bose-Einstein statistics than if they are distinguishable. We experimentally support this decade-and-a-half-old prediction by comparing indistinguishable with distinguishable photons. We use a fully programmable linear-optics platform, whose local photon statistics were shown recently to behave thermally. Our demon nondestructively measures the number of photons in a subset of the modes. Guided by the outcome, he conditionally interchanges the measured and unmeasured modes. This interchange creates a positive temperature difference between a mode in a particular subset and a mode in the other. The temperature difference is greater, on average, if the photons are indistinguishable. This result bolsters a long-standing prediction about the interplay among thermodynamics, information, and quantum particle statistics. Additionally, this work suggests a thermodynamic means of weakly validating boson-sampling platforms.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration that Maxwell's demon can create greater temperature differences with indistinguishable photons (Bose-Einstein statistics) than with distinguishable ones, supporting a long-standing quantum thermodynamics prediction.
AI.motivation: To experimentally test the decade-and-a-half-old prediction that Maxwell's demon can evolve a system farther from equilibrium with indistinguishable particles obeying Bose-Einstein statistics compared to distinguishable particles, and to explore the interplay among thermodynamics, information, and quantum particle statistics.
AI.method: Used a fully programmable linear-optics platform with thermally behaving local photon statistics. The demon nondestructively measures photon numbers in a subset of modes, then conditionally interchanges measured and unmeasured modes based on the measurement outcome, creating a temperature difference between modes in different subsets.
AI.result: The temperature difference created by the demon is greater, on average, when photons are indistinguishable compared to when they are distinguishable, experimentally supporting the theoretical prediction about quantum particle statistics enhancing thermodynamic performance.
AI.conclusion: This work provides experimental evidence for the interplay between thermodynamics, information, and quantum particle statistics, and suggests a thermodynamic approach for weakly validating boson-sampling platforms.

title: Long-Range Pairing in the Kitaev Model: Krylov Subspace Signatures
summary: Krylov subspace methods quantify operator growth in quantum many-body systems through Lanczos coefficients that encode how operators spread under time evolution. While these diagnostics have been proposed to distinguish quantum chaos from integrability, quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians are widely expected to exhibit trivial Lanczos structure. Here we demonstrate that Lanczos coefficients generated from local boundary operators provide a quantitative diagnostic of whether the lowest excitation gap is controlled by boundary-localized or bulk-extended modes in the long-range Kitaev chain, the model for topological superconductivity with algebraically decaying couplings. We introduce \emph{Krylov staggering parameter}, defined as the logarithmic ratio of consecutive odd and even Lanczos coefficients, whose sign structure correlates robustly with the edge versus bulk character of the gap across the full phase diagram. This correlation arises from a bipartite Krylov structure induced by pairing, power-law couplings, and open boundaries. We derive an exact single-particle operator Lanczos algorithm that reduces the recursion from exponentially large operator space to a finite-dimensional linear problem, achieving machine precision for chains of hundreds of sites. These results establish Krylov diagnostics as operational probes of how low-energy excitations are localized along the chain and how strongly they are tied to the boundaries with broken U(1) symmetry, with potential applications to trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Lanczos coefficients from local boundary operators in long-range Kitaev chains reveal whether the lowest excitation gap is controlled by boundary-localized or bulk-extended modes, via a novel Krylov staggering parameter that correlates with edge vs bulk character across the phase diagram.
AI.motivation: While Krylov subspace methods have been proposed to distinguish quantum chaos from integrability, quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians are widely expected to exhibit trivial Lanczos structure. The authors aim to demonstrate that Lanczos coefficients from local boundary operators can provide quantitative diagnostics of excitation localization in topological superconductors with long-range couplings.
AI.method: Introduce Krylov staggering parameter defined as logarithmic ratio of consecutive odd and even Lanczos coefficients. Develop exact single-particle operator Lanczos algorithm that reduces recursion from exponentially large operator space to finite-dimensional linear problem, enabling machine precision calculations for chains of hundreds of sites. Analyze long-range Kitaev chain with algebraically decaying couplings.
AI.result: Lanczos coefficients from boundary operators robustly correlate with edge versus bulk character of the excitation gap across the full phase diagram. The sign structure of Krylov staggering parameter indicates whether lowest excitation gap is controlled by boundary-localized or bulk-extended modes. The correlation arises from bipartite Krylov structure induced by pairing, power-law couplings, and open boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Krylov diagnostics serve as operational probes for localization of low-energy excitations along the chain and their boundary coupling strength in systems with broken U(1) symmetry. These results have potential applications to trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum simulators studying topological superconductivity.

title: Quantum nonreciprocity from qubits coupled by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction
summary: We present a theoretical study of quantum nonreciprocity induced via a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in an otherwise achiral, waveguide quantum electrodynamics. Using the full quantum master equation and input-output formalism for two-level systems coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide and driven by a coherent field, we show that an engineered DMI enables strong nonreciprocity in an otherwise reciprocal system, with tunable behavior governed by driving strength, detunings, and phase of the DMI. Using it not only demonstrates nonreciprocal transmission but also demonstrates nonreciprocal quantum entanglement and photon bunching. The system can end up in a pure state as certain decohering channels do not participate. The pure state leads to power-independent perfect transparency. Conditions are derived and depend on the propagation phase, the relative detuning of the two qubits, and the exchange interaction. At these pure-state points, the steady-state entanglement is reciprocal and admits a closed-form expression; away from them, phase control generates strong entanglement nonreciprocity. The DMI also reshapes photon statistics, redistributing two-photon correlations and shifting superbunching from transmission (no DMI) to reflection at finite DMI. These results establish DMI as a versatile resource for engineering nonreciprocity, transparency, entanglement, and photon correlations in waveguide QED, enabling isolators, routers, and superbunching light sources without requiring chiral waveguides.

AI.tldr: Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction enables strong nonreciprocity in waveguide QED systems, allowing control over transmission, entanglement, and photon statistics without chiral waveguides.
AI.motivation: To establish DMI as a versatile resource for engineering nonreciprocity in otherwise reciprocal waveguide QED systems, enabling functionalities like isolators, routers, and superbunching light sources without requiring chiral waveguides.
AI.method: Theoretical study using full quantum master equation and input-output formalism for two-level systems coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide, driven by coherent fields, with engineered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.
AI.result: DMI enables strong nonreciprocity with tunable behavior governed by driving strength, detunings, and DMI phase. System can reach pure states leading to power-independent perfect transparency. DMI reshapes photon statistics, redistributing two-photon correlations and shifting superbunching from transmission to reflection. Conditions derived for pure-state points where steady-state entanglement is reciprocal with closed-form expression; away from these points, phase control generates strong entanglement nonreciprocity.
AI.conclusion: DMI serves as a versatile resource for engineering nonreciprocity, transparency, entanglement, and photon correlations in waveguide QED, enabling practical devices like isolators, routers, and superbunching light sources without requiring chiral waveguides.

title: Resource-Scalable Fully Quantum Metropolis-Hastings for Integer Linear Programming
summary: Integer linear programming (ILP) remains computationally challenging due to its NP-complete nature despite its central role in scheduling, logistics, and design optimization. We introduce a fully quantum Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for ILP that implements a coherent random walk over the discrete feasible region using only reversible quantum circuits, without quantum-RAM assumptions or classical pre/post-processing. Each walk step is a unitary update that prepares coherent candidate moves, evaluates the objective and constraints reversibly -- including a constraint-satisfaction counter to enforce feasibility -- and encodes Metropolis acceptance amplitudes via a low-overhead linearized rule. At the logical level, the construction uses $\mathcal{O}(n\log_2 N)$ qubits to represent $n$ integer variables over the interval $[-N,\,N-1]$, and the Toffoli-equivalent cost per Metropolis step grows linearly with the total logical qubit count. Using explicit ripple-carry adder constructions, we support linear objectives and mixed equality/inequality constraints. Numerical circuit-level simulations on a broad ensemble of randomly generated instances validate the predicted linear resource scaling and exhibit progressive thermalization toward low-cost feasible solutions under the annealing schedule. Overall, the method provides a coherent, resource-characterized baseline for fully quantum constraint programming and a foundation for incorporating additional quantum speedups in combinatorial optimization.

AI.tldr: Quantum Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for integer linear programming using reversible quantum circuits without classical processing, achieving linear resource scaling with qubit count.
AI.motivation: ILP is computationally challenging (NP-complete) despite its importance in scheduling, logistics, and design optimization. Current quantum approaches often rely on quantum-RAM or classical pre/post-processing, limiting their quantum nature.
AI.method: Fully quantum Metropolis-Hastings algorithm implementing coherent random walk over discrete feasible region using only reversible quantum circuits. Uses unitary updates to prepare candidate moves, evaluate objectives/constraints reversibly with constraint-satisfaction counter, and encode Metropolis acceptance amplitudes via low-overhead linearized rule. Employs O(n log₂ N) qubits for n integer variables over [-N, N-1].
AI.result: Toffoli-equivalent cost per Metropolis step grows linearly with total logical qubit count. Numerical circuit-level simulations on random instances validate linear resource scaling and show progressive thermalization toward low-cost feasible solutions under annealing schedule.
AI.conclusion: Method provides coherent, resource-characterized baseline for fully quantum constraint programming and foundation for incorporating additional quantum speedups in combinatorial optimization.

title: The necessary and sufficient condition for perfect teleportation and superdense coding and all the suitable states for teleportation and superdense coding
summary: It is known that two local unitaries (LU) equivalent states possess the same amount of entanglement and can be used to perform the same tasks in quantum information theory (QIT). For a protocol for a task in QIT, we call a protocol LU invariant if two LU-equivalent states are either both suitable for the protocol or neither is. So far, no one has discussed whether a protocol for a task in QIT is LU invariant. In [Phys. Rev. A, 74, 062320 (2006)], Agrawal and Pati proposed the perfect teleportation protocol (PTP) and the protocol for superdense coding to transmit 2-bit classical information by sending one qubit (PSDC-2) and 3-bit classical information by sending two qubits (PSDC-3). In this paper, we show that PTP and PSDC-2 are LU invariant. That is, two LU equivalent states are suitable for PTP and PSDC-2 or neither of them is. We show that PSDC-3 is not LU invariant. We also indicate that the teleportation proposed in <cite>Nielsen</cite> is not LU invariant. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for a state to be suitable for PTP, PSDC-2, and PSDC-3, respectively. Via the LU invariance of PTP and PSDC-2, we prove that a state is suitable for PTP and PSDC-2 if and only if it has 1 ebit of shared entanglement, respectively and find all genuine entangled states and separable states which are suitable for PTP and PSDC-2, respectively. So far, no one has indicated that PTP and PSDC-2 do not require genuine entanglement. Agrawal and Pati suggested to study if there are subclasses of W SLOCC class which are suitable for PSDC-3. So far, it still remains an unsolved question. We show that any state of the SLOCC class W is not suitable for PSDC-3.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes LU (local unitary) invariance of quantum protocols, showing perfect teleportation (PTP) and 2-bit superdense coding (PSDC-2) are LU invariant, while 3-bit superdense coding (PSDC-3) is not. It establishes necessary/sufficient conditions for protocol suitability and reveals PTP/PSDC-2 don't require genuine entanglement.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether quantum information protocols are LU invariant - whether LU-equivalent states have the same suitability for protocols. Previous work proposed specific protocols but didn't examine their LU invariance properties.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis of protocol requirements, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for state suitability for PTP, PSDC-2, and PSDC-3. Examination of LU equivalence classes and their protocol suitability.
AI.result: PTP and PSDC-2 are LU invariant; PSDC-3 is not. PTP and PSDC-2 require exactly 1 ebit of shared entanglement but not genuine entanglement. No W-class states are suitable for PSDC-3.
AI.conclusion: LU invariance is protocol-dependent: PTP and PSDC-2 preserve suitability under LU equivalence, while PSDC-3 does not. This clarifies fundamental properties of quantum protocols and their entanglement requirements.

title: Extending Bell's Theorem: Nonlocality via Measurement Dependence
summary: Besides well-known conditions of locality or factorisability, deriving the Bell inequalities requires assuming that the distribution of hidden variables and Alice's and Bob's measurement settings be independent of each other. We show that (analogously to violations of locality due to action at a distance) certain violations of this Measurement Independence assumption can be associated with a notion of signalling in principle, thus making them also testable in principle, and spell out the appropriate conditions. Accordingly, we show that by imposing no-signalling one can prove a version of Bell's theorem that does not require the assumption of Measurement Independence. We discuss the "Schulman model" as an example, as well as lessons for "experimental metaphysics".

AI.tldr: The paper shows that violations of Measurement Independence (MI) can be associated with signaling in principle, making them testable, and proves a version of Bell's theorem without requiring MI by imposing no-signalling.
AI.motivation: To address the assumption of Measurement Independence in Bell inequalities and show that violations of this assumption can be linked to signaling, making them experimentally testable in principle.
AI.method: Analyzes the relationship between Measurement Independence violations and signaling, derives conditions for testability, and proves a Bell's theorem version without MI by imposing no-signalling constraints.
AI.result: Demonstrates that certain MI violations correspond to signaling in principle, establishes testability conditions, and proves a Bell's theorem that doesn't require the MI assumption when no-signalling is imposed.
AI.conclusion: Measurement Independence violations can be associated with signaling, making them testable; a Bell's theorem can be proven without MI by using no-signalling, with implications for experimental metaphysics and models like the Schulman model.

title: Multi-ion entangling gates mediated by spectrally unresolved modes
summary:
Entangling interactions between distant qubits can be mediated via an additional degree of freedom. In conventional trapped-ion schemes, realizing a well-defined, coherent gate typically requires spectrally addressing a specific bus mode. As the ion number increases, the coupling to each individual motional mode becomes weaker, so gates on large ion strings mediated by a single mode are necessarily slow. Moreover, addressing a large number of modes demands complex driving schemes, and the fundamentally perturbative character of these approaches imposes constraints on achievable gate speed and fidelity.
  Here, we introduce a scheme for entangling trapped-ion qubits using a time-dependent magnetic-field gradient, in which all axial motional modes participate in mediating the interaction and the gate construction is nonperturbative. The framework can be used to implement both multi-qubit gates and two-qubit gates between arbitrary pairs in a linear ion string. Through several explicit examples, we highlight the advantages over existing magnetic-gradient schemes and show how gates on multiple ion pairs can be carried out simultaneously.

AI.tldr: A nonperturbative trapped-ion entangling gate scheme using time-dependent magnetic-field gradients that engages all axial motional modes, enabling multi-qubit gates and simultaneous two-qubit gates on arbitrary ion pairs.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of conventional trapped-ion gate schemes where single-mode mediation becomes weak with increasing ion count, requiring slow gates, complex driving schemes, and suffering from perturbative constraints on speed and fidelity.
AI.method: Introduces a scheme using time-dependent magnetic-field gradients where all axial motional modes participate in mediating interactions, enabling nonperturbative gate construction that can implement both multi-qubit gates and two-qubit gates between arbitrary pairs in linear ion strings.
AI.result: The framework enables simultaneous gates on multiple ion pairs, offers advantages over existing magnetic-gradient schemes, and provides explicit examples demonstrating improved capabilities for large-scale quantum information processing with trapped ions.
AI.conclusion: This time-dependent magnetic-field gradient approach provides a scalable solution for high-fidelity, fast entangling gates in large trapped-ion systems by leveraging all motional modes and avoiding perturbative limitations of conventional schemes.

title: Recent Developments in VQE: Survey and Benchmarking
summary: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithm has been developed to target near term Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) computers as a method to find the eigenvalues of Hamiltonians. Unlike fully quantum algorithms such as Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE), VQE based methods are hybrid algorithms that utilize both quantum and classical hardware to combat issues with the near term quantum hardware such as small numbers of available qubits and the decoherence of qubits. Different adaptations (flavors) of VQE have been implemented to combat these scalability issues on NISQ devices compared to standard VQE. These different flavors are modifications of the underlying VQE ansatz to reduce the computational workload on the quantum hardware. In this review we focus on 3 main areas related to VQE. The first focus is on flavors of VQE that fall under the categories of circuit complexity reduction, chemistry inspired ansatz, and extensions of VQE to excited states. The remaining portion of the review focuses on benchmarking the accuracy of VQE methods and an overview of the current state of quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Review of Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) adaptations for NISQ devices, covering circuit complexity reduction, chemistry-inspired ansatz, excited state extensions, benchmarking accuracy, and quantum simulator overview.
AI.motivation: VQE has been developed for NISQ computers to find Hamiltonian eigenvalues, addressing limitations of near-term quantum hardware like limited qubits and decoherence. Different VQE adaptations are needed to combat scalability issues compared to standard VQE approaches.
AI.method: The review focuses on three main areas: 1) VQE flavors categorized as circuit complexity reduction, chemistry-inspired ansatz, and extensions to excited states; 2) benchmarking VQE method accuracy; 3) overview of current quantum simulator state.
AI.result: The paper provides a comprehensive review of VQE adaptations for NISQ devices, categorizing approaches by their strategies for reducing computational workload on quantum hardware and addressing scalability challenges.
AI.conclusion: VQE represents a crucial hybrid quantum-classical approach for NISQ-era quantum computing, with various adaptations addressing hardware limitations through circuit optimization, chemistry-specific ansatz design, excited state calculations, and systematic benchmarking.

title: Coherent states for the exotic Landau problem and related properties
summary: This work presents a comprehensive study of the exotic Landau model in a two-dimensional noncommutative plane. Beginning with the classical formulation where two conserved quantities $\mathcal{P}_i$ and $\mathcal{K}_i$ are derived, we proceed to the quantum level where these lead to two independent oscillator representations generating bosonic Fock spaces $Γ_{\mathcal{P}}$ and $Γ_{\mathcal{K}}$. Coherent states satisfying all Klauder's criteria are explicitly constructed, and their physical properties including normalization, continuity, resolution of the identity, temporal stability, and action identity are rigorously proven. We further develop matrix vector coherent states and quaternionic vector coherent states, examining their mathematical structure and physical implications. Detailed calculations of the free particle propagator via path integrals, uncertainty relations, and time evolution of probability densities are provided.

AI.tldr: Study of exotic Landau model in 2D noncommutative plane with classical conserved quantities, quantum oscillator representations, coherent states, and physical properties analysis.
AI.motivation: To investigate the exotic Landau model in a noncommutative plane, exploring its classical and quantum formulations, constructing coherent states, and analyzing physical properties in this noncommutative geometry framework.
AI.method: Classical formulation with conserved quantities P_i and K_i, quantum oscillator representations generating bosonic Fock spaces, construction of coherent states satisfying Klauder's criteria, development of matrix vector and quaternionic vector coherent states, path integral calculations for propagator, uncertainty relations, and probability density analysis.
AI.result: Successfully derived classical conserved quantities, constructed quantum oscillator representations, built coherent states satisfying all Klauder's criteria, developed matrix and quaternionic vector coherent states, calculated free particle propagator via path integrals, derived uncertainty relations, and analyzed time evolution of probability densities.
AI.conclusion: The exotic Landau model in noncommutative plane provides a rich framework with well-defined classical and quantum structures, coherent states satisfying standard criteria, and calculable physical properties including propagators and uncertainty relations.

title: Nonlinear integrated quantum photonics with AlGaAs
summary: Integrated photonics provides a powerful approach for developing compact, stable and scalable architectures for the generation, manipulation and detection of quantum states of light. To this end, several material platforms are being developed in parallel, each providing its specific assets, and hybridization techniques to combine their strengths are now possible. This review focuses on AlGaAs, a III-V semiconductor platform combining a mature fabrication technology, direct band-gap compliant with electrical injection, low-loss operation, large electro-optic effect, and compatibility with superconducting detectors for on-chip detection. We detail recent implementations of room-temperature sources of quantum light based on the high second- and third-order optical nonlinearities of the material, as well as photonic circuits embedding various functionalities ranging from polarizing beamsplitters to Mach-Zehnder interferometers, modulators and tunable filters. We then present several realizations of quantum state engineering enabled by these recent advances and discuss open perspectives and remaining challenges in the field of integrated quantum photonics with AlGaAs.

AI.tldr: Review of AlGaAs integrated photonics for quantum applications, highlighting its nonlinear optical properties, mature fabrication, and recent advances in quantum light sources and circuits.
AI.motivation: To review the AlGaAs platform's capabilities for integrated quantum photonics, leveraging its unique combination of mature fabrication, direct band-gap, low-loss operation, large electro-optic effects, and compatibility with superconducting detectors.
AI.method: Comprehensive review approach analyzing AlGaAs material properties, recent implementations of room-temperature quantum light sources using second- and third-order nonlinearities, and development of photonic circuits with various functionalities.
AI.result: AlGaAs enables high-performance quantum light sources, integrated photonic circuits with beamsplitters, interferometers, modulators, and tunable filters, and successful quantum state engineering demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: AlGaAs is a promising platform for integrated quantum photonics with demonstrated capabilities, though open challenges remain in the field's development and optimization.

title: Microscopic Origin of Superradiant Biphoton Emission in Atomic Ensembles
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Includes figures reprinted with permission from Phys. Rev. Lett. 96, 093604 (2006) and material reproduced under CC BY-NC 4.0 from APL Photonics 10, 106104 (2025)
summary: Superradiant biphoton emission from atomic ensembles provides a powerful route to generating highly correlated quantum light, yet its microscopic physical origin has remained incompletely understood. In particular, it is often unclear how collective enhancement, spontaneous emission, and vacuum fluctuations jointly give rise to both paired biphoton generation and unavoidable unpaired background within a single, self-consistent framework. Here we present a fully quantum microscopic theory within a unified Heisenberg--Langevin--Maxwell framework that explicitly incorporates dissipation and quantum noise, thereby revealing the microscopic origin of superradiant biphoton emission in atomic ensembles. The theory provides a consistent description of parametric gain and unpaired noise within the same open-quantum-system framework and applies to both Doppler-free cold atomic ensembles and Doppler-broadened warm vapors. In the high-optical-depth regime, the coupled propagation equations admit analytical solutions, under which the biphoton dynamics rigorously reduce to an effective collective two-level emission process. Within this limit, the biphoton correlation time and spectral properties are shown to obey closed-form scaling relations governed by optical depth and excited-state decoherence. Our results establish a unified microscopic picture of superradiant biphoton generation and clarify the fundamental role of vacuum fluctuations and dissipation in setting the brightness, pairing efficiency, and temporal structure of atomic biphoton sources, with direct relevance to quantum networking and atomic quantum interfaces.

AI.tldr: A unified quantum microscopic theory reveals the origin of superradiant biphoton emission in atomic ensembles, explaining how collective enhancement, dissipation, and vacuum fluctuations jointly produce both paired biphotons and unpaired background noise.
AI.motivation: The microscopic physical origin of superradiant biphoton emission from atomic ensembles remains incompletely understood, particularly regarding how collective enhancement, spontaneous emission, and vacuum fluctuations jointly give rise to both paired biphoton generation and unavoidable unpaired background within a single, self-consistent framework.
AI.method: A fully quantum microscopic theory within a unified Heisenberg-Langevin-Maxwell framework that explicitly incorporates dissipation and quantum noise, providing consistent description of parametric gain and unpaired noise within the same open-quantum-system framework, applicable to both Doppler-free cold atomic ensembles and Doppler-broadened warm vapors.
AI.result: In the high-optical-depth regime, the coupled propagation equations admit analytical solutions where biphoton dynamics reduce to an effective collective two-level emission process; biphoton correlation time and spectral properties obey closed-form scaling relations governed by optical depth and excited-state decoherence.
AI.conclusion: The theory establishes a unified microscopic picture of superradiant biphoton generation and clarifies the fundamental role of vacuum fluctuations and dissipation in setting the brightness, pairing efficiency, and temporal structure of atomic biphoton sources, with direct relevance to quantum networking and atomic quantum interfaces.

title: The Pinnacle Architecture: Reducing the cost of breaking RSA-2048 to 100 000 physical qubits using quantum LDPC codes
summary: The realisation of utility-scale quantum computing inextricably depends on the design of practical, low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures. We introduce the \textit{Pinnacle Architecture}, which uses quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes to allow for universal, fault-tolerant quantum computation with a spacetime overhead significantly smaller than that of any competing architecture. With this architecture, we show that 2048-bit RSA integers can be factored with less than one hundred thousand physical qubits, given a physical error rate of $10^{-3}$, code cycle time of $1$ \textmu s and a reaction time of $10$ \textmu s. We thereby demonstrate the feasibility of utility-scale quantum computing with an order of magnitude fewer physical qubits than has previously been believed necessary.

AI.tldr: The Pinnacle Architecture uses QLDPC codes to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing with dramatically reduced spacetime overhead, enabling 2048-bit RSA factoring with <100k physical qubits at 10^-3 error rate.
AI.motivation: Utility-scale quantum computing requires practical, low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures to overcome the resource constraints of current approaches.
AI.method: Introduces the Pinnacle Architecture based on quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes for universal, fault-tolerant quantum computation with minimal spacetime overhead.
AI.result: Demonstrates 2048-bit RSA integer factoring with less than 100,000 physical qubits given: physical error rate 10^-3, code cycle time 1μs, and reaction time 10μs.
AI.conclusion: Shows feasibility of utility-scale quantum computing with an order of magnitude fewer physical qubits than previously believed necessary, representing a significant advancement in fault-tolerant quantum architecture design.

title: Structural control of two-level defect density revealed by high-throughput correlative measurements of Josephson junctions
summary: Materials defects in Josephson junctions (JJs), often referred to as two-level systems (TLS), couple to superconducting qubits and are a critical bottleneck for scalable quantum processors. Despite their importance, understanding the microscopic sources of TLS and how to mitigate them has remained a major challenge. Here, we demonstrate a high-throughput, correlated approach to trace the microstructural origins of strongly-coupled TLS in Josephson circuits. We assembled a massive dataset of TLS across 6,000 Al/AlOx/Al JJs and more than 600 atomic resolution transmission electron microscopy images. We statistically link fabrication, microstructure, and TLS occurrence, revealing a strong correlation between Al electrode thickness, Al grain size, and TLS density. Correspondingly, we find a two-thirds reduction in TLS prompted by a change in electrode fabrication parameters. These results demonstrate a robust, data-driven methodology to understand and control defects in quantum circuits and pave the way for significantly reducing TLS density.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a high-throughput approach linking fabrication parameters, microstructure, and TLS density in Josephson junctions, finding strong correlations between electrode thickness, grain size, and TLS occurrence, leading to a two-thirds reduction in TLS density.
AI.motivation: Two-level systems (TLS) in Josephson junctions are critical defects that couple to superconducting qubits and represent a major bottleneck for scalable quantum processors. Despite their importance, the microscopic origins of TLS and methods for mitigating them have remained poorly understood.
AI.method: High-throughput, correlated approach combining massive datasets: 6,000 Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junctions and over 600 atomic-resolution transmission electron microscopy images. Statistical analysis linking fabrication parameters, microstructure, and TLS occurrence.
AI.result: Strong correlation between Al electrode thickness, Al grain size, and TLS density. A two-thirds reduction in TLS achieved by changing electrode fabrication parameters. Demonstration of robust data-driven methodology for understanding and controlling quantum circuit defects.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a systematic approach to trace microstructural origins of TLS in Josephson circuits, enabling significant reduction of TLS density and paving the way for improved quantum processor scalability through defect control.

title: Control the qubit-qubit coupling with double superconducting resonators
summary: We experimentally studied the switching off processes in the double-resonator coupler superconducting quantum circuit.In both frequency and time-domain, we observed the variation of qubit-qubit effective coupling by tuning qubits'frequencies. According to the measurement results, by just shifting qubits' frequencies smaller than 50 MHz, the effective qubit-qubit coupling strength can be tuned from switching off point to two qubit gate point (effective coupling larger than 5 MHz) in double-resonator superconducting quantum circuit. The double-resonator coupler superconducting quantum circuit has the advantage of simple fabrications, introducing less flux noises, reducing occupancy of dilution refrigerator cables, which might supply a promising platform for future large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of tunable qubit-qubit coupling in a double-resonator superconducting quantum circuit, showing effective coupling can be switched from off-state to two-qubit gate operation with minimal frequency tuning.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable superconducting quantum processor platform with simplified fabrication, reduced flux noise sensitivity, and minimized cryogenic wiring requirements by using a double-resonator coupler architecture.
AI.method: Experimental study of switching off processes in double-resonator coupler superconducting quantum circuits using both frequency and time-domain measurements, tuning qubit frequencies to vary effective qubit-qubit coupling.
AI.result: Effective qubit-qubit coupling strength can be tuned from switching off point to two-qubit gate operation (effective coupling >5 MHz) by shifting qubit frequencies less than 50 MHz, demonstrating precise control in the double-resonator architecture.
AI.conclusion: The double-resonator coupler superconducting quantum circuit offers advantages in fabrication simplicity, reduced flux noise, and minimized cryogenic wiring, making it a promising platform for future large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

title: Scalable and Highly Fault-Tolerant Circular Quantum Byzantine Agreement
summary: Quantum Byzantine Agreement (QBA), a cornerstone of quantum blockchain, offers inherent advantages in security and fault tolerance over classical protocols, guaranteed by the laws of quantum mechanics. However, existing multiparty QBA protocols face challenges for large-scale deployment due to exponential communication complexity or reliance on complex multi-particle entanglement. To address this, we propose a multiparty circular QBA protocol that adopts a semi-decentralized architecture, leveraging circular message gathering and quantum digital signatures to achieve quadratic communication complexity and enhanced fault tolerance. Our protocol is experimentally feasible, requiring only weak coherent states, and is compatible with existing star-shaped quantum networks. Simulations conducted on a global satellite-to-ground network demonstrate that the protocol sustains high consensus rates among multiple users, even when employing different key generation protocols under realistic conditions. This work presents a scalable framework for large-scale QBA networks, establishing the foundation for a practical quantum blockchain that enables secure and fault-tolerant decentralized services.

AI.tldr: A scalable multiparty Quantum Byzantine Agreement protocol with quadratic communication complexity using circular message gathering and quantum digital signatures, experimentally feasible with weak coherent states.
AI.motivation: Existing multiparty QBA protocols face challenges for large-scale deployment due to exponential communication complexity or reliance on complex multi-particle entanglement, limiting practical implementation in quantum blockchain applications.
AI.method: Proposes a multiparty circular QBA protocol with semi-decentralized architecture using circular message gathering and quantum digital signatures, requiring only weak coherent states and compatible with existing star-shaped quantum networks.
AI.result: Protocol achieves quadratic communication complexity and enhanced fault tolerance; simulations on global satellite-to-ground networks demonstrate high consensus rates among multiple users under realistic conditions with different key generation protocols.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a scalable framework for large-scale QBA networks, establishing foundation for practical quantum blockchain enabling secure and fault-tolerant decentralized services.

title: Rapid Dissipative Ground State Preparation at Chemical Transition States
summary: Simulating chemical reactions is a central challenge in computational chemistry, characterized by an uneven difficulty profile: while equilibrium reactant and product geometries are often classically tractable, intermediate transition states frequently exhibit strong correlation that defies standard approximations. We present a protocol for dissipative ground state preparation that exploits this structure by treating the reaction path itself as a computational primitive. Our protocol uses an approach where a state prepared at a tractable geometry is propagated along a discretized reaction coordinate using Procrustes-aligned orbital rotations and stabilized by engineered dissipative cooling. We show that for reaction paths satisfying a localized Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) drift condition in the strongly correlated regime, the algorithm prepares ground states of chemical systems with $N_o$ orbitals to an energy error $ε_E$ with a total gate complexity scaling as $\widetilde{O}(N_o^{3}/ε_E)$. We provide logical resource estimates for benchmark systems including FeMoco, Cytochrome P450, and Ru-based carbon capture catalysts.

AI.tldr: Protocol for quantum simulation of chemical reactions using dissipative ground state preparation along reaction paths, achieving $\widetilde{O}(N_o^{3}/ε_E)$ gate complexity for strongly correlated transition states.
AI.motivation: Chemical reaction simulation faces uneven difficulty: equilibrium geometries are classically tractable, but intermediate transition states exhibit strong correlation that defies standard approximations, requiring quantum approaches.
AI.method: Dissipative ground state preparation protocol that treats reaction path as computational primitive. Propagates state from tractable geometry along discretized reaction coordinate using Procrustes-aligned orbital rotations, stabilized by engineered dissipative cooling.
AI.result: For reaction paths satisfying localized Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) drift condition in strongly correlated regime, algorithm prepares ground states with $\widetilde{O}(N_o^{3}/ε_E)$ gate complexity. Provides logical resource estimates for FeMoco, Cytochrome P450, and Ru-based carbon capture catalysts.
AI.conclusion: Protocol enables efficient quantum simulation of chemical reactions by exploiting the reaction path structure, addressing the challenge of strongly correlated transition states with favorable scaling and practical resource estimates.

title: The Power of Two Bases: Robust and copy-optimal certification of nearly all quantum states with few-qubit measurements
summary:
A central task in quantum information science is state certification: testing whether an unknown state is $ε_1$-close to a fixed target state, or $ε_2$-far. Recent work has shown that surprisingly simple measurement protocols--comprising only single-qubit measurements--suffice to certify arbitrary $n$-qubit states [Huang, Preskill, Soleimanifar '25; Gupta, He, O'Donnell '25]. However, these certification protocols are not robust: rather than allowing constant $ε_1$, they can only positively certify states within $ε_1=O(1/n)$ trace distance of the target. In many experimental settings, the appropriate error tolerance is constant as the system size grows, so this lack of robustness renders existing tests inapplicable at scale, no matter how many times the test is repeated.
  Here we present robust certification protocols based on few-qubit measurements that apply to all but a $O(2^{-n})$-fraction of pure target states. Our first protocol achieves constant robustness, i.e. $ε_1=Θ(1)$, using a single $O(\log n)$-qubit measurement along with single-qubit measurements in the $Z$ or $X$ basis on the other qubits. As a corollary of its robustness, this protocol also achieves constant (in $n$) copy complexity, which is optimal. Our second protocol uses exclusively single-qubit measurements and is nearly robust: $ε_1=Ω(1/\log n)$. Our tests are based on a new uncertainty principle for conditional fidelities, which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Robust quantum state certification protocols using few-qubit measurements that achieve constant error tolerance for most pure states, overcoming previous limitations of O(1/n) robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing single-qubit measurement protocols for quantum state certification lack robustness - they only work for states within O(1/n) trace distance of the target, making them inapplicable for constant error tolerance at scale despite repeated testing.
AI.method: Two protocols based on new uncertainty principle for conditional fidelities: 1) Uses single O(log n)-qubit measurement plus single-qubit Z/X basis measurements on other qubits; 2) Uses exclusively single-qubit measurements.
AI.result: First protocol achieves constant robustness (ε₁=Θ(1)) for all but O(2⁻ⁿ)-fraction of pure states with optimal constant copy complexity. Second protocol achieves near-constant robustness (ε₁=Ω(1/log n)) using only single-qubit measurements.
AI.conclusion: Robust certification protocols enable practical quantum state verification at scale with constant error tolerance, overcoming fundamental limitations of previous approaches through novel uncertainty principles and measurement strategies.

title: Experimental challenges and prospects for quantum-enhanced energy conversion: Stationary Fano coherence in V-type qutrits interacting with polarized incoherent radiation
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures. Comments and feedback are welcome
summary: Quantum coherence offers potential for energy conversion technologies. It influences light absorption and emission, affecting energy conversion limits and efficiency. As a result, quantum coherence is being harnessed to boost performance in quantum heat engines, photocells, and photosynthetic-inspired platforms. Of particular interest in this context is the generation of Fano coherences, i.e., the formation of quantum coherences due to the interaction with the continuum of modes characterizing an incoherent process. We aim to formalize mathematically the possibility of achieving steady-state Fano coherence in a V-type three-level quantum system using polarized incoherent radiation, without requiring the energy difference between the excited levels to tend to zero. We perform this analysis by deriving the Bloch-Redfield equation from first-principles by quantizing the incoherent radiation. The resulting reduced dynamics of the system are analysed, so as to determine the lifetime of Fano coherence and identify the conditions under which it becomes stationary. We characterise distinct dynamical regimes, ranging from weak to strong pumping, in which steady-state Fano coherence emerges, and we quantitatively determine its magnitude. For each regime, we analyse the generation of Fano coherence as a function of both the intensity of the incoherent pumping and the energy splitting between the excited levels. We also assess how obtaining Fano coherence is modified by symmetric or asymmetric decay rates. These findings indicate that a three-level quantum system driven by polarized incoherent light can act as a robust resource for coherence-assisted energy conversion and storage. Finally, we discuss the experimental challenges associated with the implementation of the proposed model using an ensemble of Rubidium atoms.

AI.tldr: A theoretical study shows how polarized incoherent radiation can generate steady-state Fano coherences in V-type three-level quantum systems, enabling robust quantum coherence for energy conversion applications.
AI.motivation: Quantum coherence offers potential for enhancing energy conversion technologies, particularly through Fano coherences formed via interaction with incoherent processes. The paper aims to formalize how steady-state Fano coherence can be achieved in V-type three-level systems using polarized incoherent radiation without requiring degenerate excited levels.
AI.method: Derived Bloch-Redfield equation from first principles by quantizing incoherent radiation. Analyzed reduced dynamics of V-type three-level system to determine Fano coherence lifetime and stationary conditions. Characterized distinct dynamical regimes (weak to strong pumping) and examined coherence generation as function of pumping intensity and excited level energy splitting.
AI.result: Identified conditions for steady-state Fano coherence emergence across different pumping regimes. Quantitatively determined coherence magnitude and analyzed effects of symmetric/asymmetric decay rates. Found that three-level systems driven by polarized incoherent light can serve as robust resources for coherence-assisted energy conversion and storage.
AI.conclusion: Theoretical framework demonstrates feasibility of generating steady-state Fano coherences in V-type quantum systems using polarized incoherent radiation, providing a pathway for practical implementation in quantum-enhanced energy technologies. Discussed experimental challenges for implementation with Rubidium atom ensembles.

title: Learning functions of quantum states with distributed architectures
summary: Distributed architectures are gaining prominence in quantum machine learning as a means to overcome hardware limitations and enable scalable quantum information processing. In this context, we analyze the design and performance of distributed Quantum Extreme Learning Machine (QELM) architectures for learning functions of quantum states directly from data, restricting measurements to easily implementable projective measurements in the computational basis. The aim is to determine which schemes can effectively recover specific properties of input quantum states, including both linear and nonlinear features, while also quantifying the resource requirements in terms of measurements and reservoir dimensionality. We compare standard three-layer QELM with a spatially multiplexed architecture composed of multiple independent three-layer units for linear (quantum) tasks, showing a linear reduction in resource requirements per unit. For nonlinear properties, the study examines the multiple-injection architecture and introduces a novel distributed design that incorporates entanglement between subsystems within a spatially multiplexed framework, evaluating its performance through the reconstruction of complex nonlinear quantities such as polynomial targets, Rényi entropy, and entanglement measures. Our results demonstrate that the distributed design enables the reconstruction of higher-order nonlinearities by increasing the number of interacting subsystems with reduced resources, rather than increasing the size of an individual reservoir, providing a scalable and hardware-efficient route to quantum property learning.

AI.tldr: Distributed QELM architectures enable scalable quantum property learning with reduced resource requirements by using multiple interacting subsystems instead of larger individual reservoirs.
AI.motivation: To overcome hardware limitations in quantum machine learning and enable scalable quantum information processing by developing distributed architectures that can effectively recover both linear and nonlinear properties of quantum states with practical measurement constraints.
AI.method: Analyzed distributed QELM architectures using computational basis projective measurements. Compared standard three-layer QELM with spatially multiplexed architectures for linear tasks. For nonlinear properties, examined multiple-injection architecture and introduced novel distributed design with entanglement between subsystems in spatially multiplexed framework. Evaluated performance through reconstruction of polynomial targets, Rényi entropy, and entanglement measures.
AI.result: Distributed design enables reconstruction of higher-order nonlinearities by increasing number of interacting subsystems with reduced resources rather than increasing individual reservoir size. Spatially multiplexed architecture shows linear reduction in resource requirements per unit for linear tasks.
AI.conclusion: Distributed QELM architectures provide a scalable and hardware-efficient route to quantum property learning, particularly effective for recovering complex nonlinear properties of quantum states while minimizing resource requirements.

title: Operational limits to entanglement-based satellite quantum key distribution
comment: 19 pages, 1 table, 9 figures including supplementary files. Comments welcome
summary: Space-based distribution of quantum entanglement will be essential for global quantum networking and secure communications. Modelling and analysis of the performance of satellite entanglement pair distribution is important for the architecture and design of constellations and space systems. Entanglement-based quantum key distribution, in the absence of quantum repeaters, is especially prone to finite key effects due to low coincident count rates compared to trusted node single-path links. Therefore, there is a need for a comprehensive study of finite-key effects in the context of direct dual downlink quantum key distribution taking into account the characteristics of the overpass geometries. We develop a high-fidelity model of pair distribution from a low Earth orbit satellite that captures orbital dynamics, elevation-dependent loss, background noise, and extraneous detector effects. We integrate this with a rigorous finite-key security framework for the BBM92 protocol to optimise secret key length across different overpass geometries, orbital altitudes, and optical ground station (OGS) separations. These results provide quantitative performance bounds and design guidelines for near-term SatQKD missions, enabling informed trade-offs between satellite payload complexity, ground infrastructure, and achievable secure key throughput.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a comprehensive model for satellite-based quantum entanglement distribution, integrating orbital dynamics with finite-key security analysis to optimize quantum key distribution performance for near-term satellite missions.
AI.motivation: Satellite-based quantum entanglement distribution is crucial for global quantum networks, but current systems face challenges with finite-key effects due to low coincident count rates compared to trusted node links. There's a need for comprehensive modeling that accounts for overpass geometries and orbital dynamics to optimize performance.
AI.method: Developed a high-fidelity model of entanglement pair distribution from LEO satellites capturing orbital dynamics, elevation-dependent loss, background noise, and detector effects. Integrated this with rigorous finite-key security framework for BBM92 protocol to optimize secret key length across different overpass geometries, altitudes, and ground station separations.
AI.result: The model provides quantitative performance bounds and design guidelines for near-term SatQKD missions, enabling informed trade-offs between satellite payload complexity, ground infrastructure, and achievable secure key throughput.
AI.conclusion: The integrated modeling approach offers essential tools for designing and optimizing satellite quantum key distribution systems, addressing critical finite-key effects while considering practical orbital and ground station constraints for real-world deployment.

title: Single-shot GHZ characterization with connectivity-aware fanout constructions
summary: We propose a practical recipe to transform any depth-$L$ block of CNOTs that prepares $n$-qubit GHZ states into an $n$-qubit fanout gate (multitarget-CNOT) of depth $2L-1$, without the need for ancilla qubits. Considering known logarithmic-depth circuits to prepare GHZ-states, this allows us to construct an $n$-qubit fanout gate with depth $2\log_2(n)-1$, reproducing previous ancillaless constructions. We employ our recipe to construct $n$-qubit fanout gates under heavy-hex connectivity restrictions, obtaining a depth of $O(n^{1/2})$, again reproducing previous complexity theory constructions. Using this recipe on the \textit{ibm\_fez} architecture yields a $156$-qubit fanout construction with depth $33$. Additionally, we show how to employ these $n$-qubit fanout constructions to measure complete sets of commuting observables from the $n$-body Pauli group with the same depth, allowing for efficient single-shot characterization of any GHZ-like state in a given known basis, e.g. fully characterizing a single copy of a $156$-qubit GHZ state using circuit depth $33$ in $\textit{ibm\_fez}$ (its preparation requires an additional depth of $17$).

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method to convert any depth-L CNOT circuit preparing n-qubit GHZ states into an n-qubit fanout gate (multitarget-CNOT) with depth 2L-1 without ancilla qubits, enabling efficient construction of fanout gates and measurement of commuting Pauli observables.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop efficient ancilla-free constructions of n-qubit fanout gates (multitarget-CNOT operations) that are crucial for quantum computing applications, particularly for measuring complete sets of commuting observables and characterizing GHZ-like states efficiently.
AI.method: The method provides a practical recipe to transform any depth-L block of CNOTs that prepares n-qubit GHZ states into an n-qubit fanout gate of depth 2L-1 without requiring ancilla qubits. This transformation leverages known logarithmic-depth GHZ-state preparation circuits and adapts them to specific connectivity constraints like heavy-hex architectures.
AI.result: The recipe produces n-qubit fanout gates with depth 2log₂(n)-1 for general connectivity, matching previous ancilla-free constructions. Under heavy-hex connectivity restrictions, it achieves depth O(n¹/²), reproducing previous complexity theory results. On the ibm_fez architecture, a 156-qubit fanout gate is constructed with depth 33. The method also enables measurement of complete sets of commuting observables from the n-body Pauli group with the same depth, allowing efficient single-shot characterization of GHZ-like states.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a versatile recipe for constructing efficient ancilla-free fanout gates that can be adapted to various connectivity constraints, enabling practical implementation of n-qubit fanout operations and efficient characterization of GHZ-like states on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Universal Sequential Changepoint Detection of Quantum Observables via Classical Shadows
summary: We study sequential quantum changepoint detection in settings where the pre- and post-change regimes are specified through constraints on the expectation values of a finite set of observables. We consider an architecture with separate measurement and detection modules, and assume that the observables relevant to the detector are unknown to the measurement device. For this scenario, we introduce shadow-based sequential changepoint e-detection (eSCD), a novel protocol that combines a universal measurement strategy based on classical shadows with a nonparametric sequential test built on e-detectors. Classical shadows provide universality with respect to the detector's choice of observables, while the e-detector framework enables explicit control of the average run length (ARL) to false alarm. Under an ARL constraint, we establish finite-sample guarantees on the worst-case expected detection delay of eSCD. Numerical experiments validate the theory and demonstrate that eSCD achieves performance competitive with observable-specific measurement strategies, while retaining full measurement universality.

AI.tldr: Shadow-based sequential changepoint e-detection (eSCD) protocol combines classical shadows for universal measurement with e-detectors for controlled false alarm rates in quantum changepoint detection.
AI.motivation: Address sequential quantum changepoint detection when pre- and post-change regimes are defined by expectation value constraints of observables, and the detector's observables are unknown to the measurement device.
AI.method: eSCD protocol: uses classical shadows for universal measurement strategy (independent of detector's observables) combined with nonparametric sequential test built on e-detectors for explicit ARL control.
AI.result: Established finite-sample guarantees on worst-case expected detection delay under ARL constraint; numerical experiments show eSCD achieves performance competitive with observable-specific strategies while maintaining full measurement universality.
